# Replaced busted brake line but the brakes still don't work

Replacing a physical component like a corroded brake line often feels like a binary success or failure event: either the metal is swapped, or it isn't. However, in hydraulic systems, swapping a single part rarely guarantees system-wide functionality if the diagnostic approach treats the vehicle as an isolated unit rather than an integrated circuit. The scenario you described—replacing a 2003 Chevrolet Avalanche brake line, adding fluid, and bleeding for an hour with no improvement—is a classic symptom of either trapped air in a specific reservoir pocket or a compromised master cylinder, not necessarily a failure to bleed the system adequately.

Bleeding brakes for an hour is excessive for a standard replacement unless there was catastrophic contamination or multiple disconnected lines simultaneously repaired. When you release pressure on the pedal and the brake service engine light illuminates immediately, the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) is detecting a specific threshold violation. In modern GM platforms like the Avalanche, this usually indicates that pedal travel has exceeded a predefined limit before the hydraulic pressure builds to a safe operating range. This isn't just "air in the lines"; it's often a sign that the master cylinder itself is bypassing fluid internally or that the accumulator spring within the brake booster assembly isn't generating sufficient vacuum assist.

Consider the internal architecture of the dual-circuit master cylinder on this vehicle model. These units contain two separate pistons for the front and rear circuits, separated by a dry partition wall. If one side has been compromised by heat damage from nearby components or chemical degradation over 20 years of service, replacing the external line does nothing to seal the internal bypass. When you pump the pedal, fluid might be entering the reservoir instead of pushing against the wheel cylinders. The result is a spongy pedal that travels to the floor because the hydraulic multiplier effect never engages.

To diagnose this without relying solely on time-based bleeding, you must verify fluid displacement and pressure consistency. Disconnect the bleeder screw on the lowest circuit (typically rear right or left) while an assistant applies steady pressure to the brake pedal. If you see a consistent stream of clear fluid with no bubbles after the first few pumps, but the pedal still sinks, the issue is almost certainly internal leakage in the master cylinder. Conversely, if air continues to escape despite proper bleeding techniques—such as using a vacuum extractor rather than gravity or pump methods—the caliper pistons may be seized, creating a closed loop that traps air pockets near the caliper seals.

Another possibility involves the proportioning valve or the emergency brake switch, though these typically cause drag or light issues rather than total pedal failure. However, on this specific chassis, the Electronic Brake Control System (EBCM) monitors pedal position via potentiometers. If the mechanical linkage is disconnected or the sensor wiring is damaged during line replacement, the EBCM cannot confirm pedal depression and will trigger the service warning immediately upon release.

The most reliable path forward is to inspect the master cylinder bore for scoring or seal failure. If the internal seals are bypassing fluid, no amount of bleeding will restore function because the system is short-circuiting before it reaches the wheels. In cases where the master cylinder is the culprit, replacing the line and bleeding the system becomes a moot exercise until the source of the volume loss is addressed.
